title: Educational Technology Research

pts: EdTech marketing claims frequently outpace the actual, careful research evidence supporting a given tool's effectiveness.
This connects directly to Unit 81's critical-research-reading skill, applied specifically to evaluating EdTech vendor claims.
Independent, peer-reviewed evaluation, where available, offers more reliable evidence than vendor-produced studies.

v: Two or three EdTech advertisements or product web pages

items: Collect marketing claims from two or three English-learning products.
For each claim, ask: What exactly is claimed? What evidence is offered? Who produced it? Was it peer-reviewed? Were learners like ours studied?
Search for any independent study of the product (Unit 81).
Rate each claim: supported, partly supported, or unsupported.
Rewrite one claim so that it matches the evidence honestly.
With B2–C1 learners, run this as a critical-reading lesson on persuasive language (Unit 59).
Support: provide a claim card with the five questions printed.
Challenge: find a vendor-funded study and identify the features that could bias its results.

blocks.x: A claim and its honest rewrite (both written for this book):

lines: Advertisement: Our AI tutor makes learners fluent in 30 days, proven by research!
Evidence offered: a company survey of 500 users reporting they ‘felt more confident’.
Honest rewrite: In a company survey, many users said they felt more confident after a month. We have not yet tested whether their English improved.

blocks.x: Confidence is worth having, but it is not the same as proficiency, and a self-selected sample of enthusiastic users is not a representative group.

body: Purpose: to show the distance between marketing and evidence. Content: a tall billboard labelled ‘claims’ beside a short stack of papers labelled ‘independent evidence’, with a measuring tape showing the gap. Style: light, slightly humorous. Board version: a tall and a short bar.

items: Google Scholar (free) and ERIC (free) for independent studies.

blocks.x: Printed advertisements from newspapers and a paper claim card.

pts: Adaptive platforms that adjust content difficulty based on learner performance show some genuine, if modest, evidence of effectiveness for discrete skill practice.
This connects to Unit 18's automated-feedback discussion — adaptive systems work best for grammar and vocabulary, less well for communicative competence.
Effectiveness varies considerably by specific platform and implementation quality, resisting broad generalisation.

v: 15 minutes a day over four weeks
A spaced-repetition app, or a paper Leitner box

items: Select 60 high-frequency words from the current coursebook units (Unit 5).
Learners practise them in short daily sessions using an adaptive flashcard system that repeats difficult words more often.
Once a week, learners use the words in a communicative task, such as a picture description in pairs.
At the end of four weeks, test recognition and use in a short writing task.
Discuss with learners what the app helped with and what it did not.
Learners without phones use a paper Leitner box: cards move to a less frequent box when answered correctly.
Support: start with 30 words and pictures.
Challenge: learners add collocations and example sentences to each card.

lines: S1: The app helped me remember the meanings. I got 55 out of 60.
S2: But when I wrote the story, I couldn’t use ‘although’ correctly.
T: So the app helped with recognition. Using words in sentences needed the pair task and feedback.

blocks.x: Adaptive systems are well suited to discrete practice such as vocabulary and grammar forms; communicative competence still needs interaction and feedback (Unit 18).

body: Purpose: to show where adaptive tools fit. Content: a two-column chart; ‘discrete practice’ (vocabulary, spelling, grammar forms) with a device icon, and ‘communicative use’ (discussion, negotiation, writing for readers) with a group of learners. Style: clear. Board version: two columns.

items: Anki (free on desktop and Android; paid on iOS) or Quizlet (free plan with limits) for spaced repetition.

blocks.x: A paper Leitner box made from an envelope or shoebox with three sections.

body: The Leitner box, a paper system for spaced practice, was described decades before smartphone apps. Many ‘adaptive’ flashcard apps automate the same principle: review what you find hard more often, and what you know less often.

pts: AI conversation practice tools show promise for extending speaking practice opportunity, connecting to Unit 84's earlier discussion.
Rigorous, independent research on these newer tools' actual learning impact remains limited relative to their rapid market growth.
This is a genuinely fast-moving research area where current findings may need frequent revision.

v: 20 minutes a week for three weeks
An AI chatbot with voice or text; a paper log

items: Check the tool’s age requirements, privacy terms and school policy before use.
Learners hold a ten-minute conversation with an AI partner on a set topic, for example planning a trip to Mysuru.
They log new words, corrections received and moments when the conversation felt unnatural.
In class, pairs compare logs and repeat the conversation with each other.
After three weeks, discuss what AI practice added and what human conversation offered that AI did not.
Use the AI as a rehearsal partner before a class role-play (Unit 38).
Support: provide opening questions and useful phrases.
Challenge: learners ask the AI to play a difficult role, for example a sceptical interviewer.

blocks.x: A learner’s log entry (written for this book):

lines: New words: ‘itinerary’, ‘heritage site’. Correction: I said ‘I am going there since two years’; the AI suggested ‘I have been going there for two years’.
Unnatural moment: it never interrupted me or misunderstood me, so I didn’t practise asking for repetition.

blocks.x: Independent research on these tools’ learning impact is still limited compared with their rapid spread, so conclusions drawn now may need revising soon.

body: Purpose: to compare AI and human practice. Content: a learner between a screen and a classmate; labels on the screen side read ‘always available’ and ‘patient’; on the human side ‘real misunderstandings’ and ‘shared context’. Style: balanced. Board version: two circles with labels.

items: ChatGPT, Gemini or Microsoft Copilot (free tiers; age limits and data policies apply) with voice or text.

blocks.x: Paired conversation cards with prompts, practised with a classmate.

pts: Gamified language-learning apps show genuine engagement benefits, with more mixed evidence for deep, lasting proficiency gains.
This connects to Unit 22's motivation research — gamification often works through extrinsic reward mechanisms with their own genuine limitations.
Engagement and genuine learning outcome are related but distinct measures, worth evaluating separately.

v: A gamified quiz platform or paper game; a short delayed test

items: Teach a set of 20 phrasal verbs with two class groups (or two halves of one class).
Group A reviews with a fast gamified quiz with points and a leader board; Group B reviews with a paper retrieval task in pairs.
Ask both groups to rate how much they enjoyed the review (1–5).
Two weeks later, give both groups the same short test without warning.
Compare enjoyment and test results, and discuss what the difference might mean.
Repeat with the groups reversed to reduce the effect of group differences.
Support: fewer items with pictures.
Challenge: learners design the paper retrieval task.

lines: Group A enjoyment 4.6; delayed test 11/20.
Group B enjoyment 3.4; delayed test 12/20.
T: What can we conclude?
S1: The game was more fun.
S2: But it didn’t help more. Maybe we were thinking about points, not words.
T: Perhaps. With one small test, we can’t be sure; we would need to repeat it.

blocks.x: Points and badges are extrinsic rewards, and research on rewards shows they can sometimes reduce intrinsic motivation for an activity (Deci, Koestner and Ryan 1999; see Unit 22). Engagement and learning are worth measuring separately.

body: Purpose: to separate engagement from learning. Content: two dials side by side, one labelled ‘engagement’ and one ‘learning that lasts’, pointing to different values. Style: clean. Board version: two semicircles with needles.

items: Kahoot! or Wayground (formerly Quizizz; free basic plans) [VERIFY current name and plan] for gamified review; Google Forms (free) for the delayed test.

blocks.x: A paper quiz with team points on the board.

pts: Ask what specific evidence supports this tool's claims, whether that evidence is independent, and whether it matches your specific learner population.
This directly applies Unit 81's critical-research-reading framework to a genuinely practical, frequent professional decision.
This connects to Unit 67's action-research approach — piloting and evaluating a new tool in your own context provides the most directly relevant evidence.

v: An evaluation checklist; one class; a baseline test

items: State what the tool is supposed to improve, in measurable terms.
Apply a checklist: What is the evidence? Is it independent? Were learners like ours studied? Does it work offline or on low data? What does it cost? What happens to learners’ data?
Give a short baseline test or collect baseline work.
Use the tool with one class for four to six weeks, keeping a brief log of problems.
Repeat the test or task and compare with a similar class that did not use the tool, or with the baseline.
Decide: adopt, adapt or abandon, and share the result (Unit 67).
Several schools in a cluster pilot the same tool and pool their results.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A pilot summary (written for this book):

lines: Tool: a phonics app for Class 3. Aim: improve decoding of CVC words. Result: decoding scores rose by a similar amount in the pilot class and the comparison class. Log: the app needed data, and half the learners could use it only in school.
Decision: adapt. Keep the app for the school computer corner; do not require it at home.

blocks.x: Local pilots are small, but they answer the question vendors’ studies cannot: does it work here, with our learners?

body: Purpose: to show a pilot as a decision process. Content: a flow from ‘Claim’ to ‘Checklist’ to ‘Pilot’ to ‘Compare’, then three exits: adopt, adapt, abandon. Style: flowchart. Board version: boxes and arrows.

items: Google Sheets (free) for baseline and post-test scores.

blocks.x: A paper checklist and results table in the research journal.

pts: Teacher beliefs about technology's value significantly shape how genuinely, versus superficially, a new EdTech tool gets implemented.
This connects directly to the teacher-cognition research from Unit 79, applied specifically to technology-adoption decisions.
Institutional EdTech mandates without genuine teacher buy-in often produce disappointing, superficial implementation.

v: A belief questionnaire (written for this book); chart paper

items: Teachers respond anonymously to belief statements about technology and learning.
Display the pattern of responses.
Discuss the difference between first-order barriers (devices, connectivity, time) and second-order barriers (beliefs about teaching and learning) (Ertmer and Ottenbreit-Leftwich 2010).
In groups, analyse one technology mandate the group has experienced: what went well, and why?
Agree one support that would help teachers use a tool purposefully, not just to comply.
Pair the questionnaire with a classroom observation of one technology-supported lesson (Unit 68).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Technology mainly helps learners practise what I have already taught.
If learners use phones in class, I lose control.
Technology can help learners do things they could not do otherwise.
A: We were told to upload videos to the platform every week, so we did. Nobody watched them.
B: Because it was about compliance, not about what learners needed.

blocks.x: Teacher beliefs, shaped by experience and school culture, influence how technology is actually used (Unit 79).

body: Purpose: to show first- and second-order barriers. Content: a wall with a visible lower layer labelled ‘devices, data, time’ and a hidden upper layer labelled ‘beliefs, confidence, culture’. Style: simple. Board version: two rows of bricks.

items: Google Forms (free) for an anonymous belief questionnaire; DIKSHA (free, Government of India) as a shared example platform.

blocks.x: Paper questionnaires and a sticky-note display.

pts: Much EdTech research examines short-term outcomes; genuinely long-term proficiency and retention research remains comparatively rare.
This connects to Unit 89's attrition-and-maintenance content — does a given tool support genuine, durable learning, or just short-term performance?
This gap argues for appropriate caution about strong long-term effectiveness claims for any specific technology.

v: 30 minutes planning; tests over three months
Items from a recent technology-supported unit

items: After a technology-supported unit, give the normal end-of-unit test.
Keep a parallel set of items.
Give the parallel test four weeks later, and again after three months, without warning.
Compare the three results.
Discuss what supports retention: spaced review, use in communication, or both (Unit 89).
Compare retention for items learned through an app and items learned through class activities.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: End of unit: 78%. After four weeks: 61%. After three months: 52%.
Items also used in a class project: 74% after three months.

blocks.x: Much technology research measures short-term outcomes, and strong claims about long-term effects need caution (Banerjee et al. 2007). A delayed test is a simple, honest way for teachers to check.

body: Purpose: to show retention over time. Content: a line graph falling from the end-of-unit score, with a second, flatter line for items used in communication. Style: clear chart. Board version: two lines on a simple axis.

items: Google Forms (free) for parallel tests; Google Sheets (free) for the graph.

blocks.x: Paper tests and a hand-drawn line graph.

body: Build a small bank of parallel test items for every unit you teach. They cost little to make and give you your own long-term evidence about what learners keep.

pts: Educational technology offers genuine, evidence-supported value in specific, well-matched applications, without justifying uncritical wholesale adoption.
This mirrors Unit 84's AI-specific conclusion, generalised to educational technology as a broader category.
Informed, evidence-responsive evaluation, applied consistently, remains the right professional stance across this entire domain.

v: Outcomes of points 1–7; a policy template

items: List the technologies currently used in your department or DIET.
For each, note the evidence you have (independent, local pilot or none).
Draft principles: purpose before tool; independent evidence where possible; local pilots; offline alternatives; data protection; attention to equity.
Decide which tools to continue, pilot or stop.
Agree when the policy will be reviewed.
Invite learners’ views on which tools help them most.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: We use technology when it serves a clear learning purpose, not because it is new.
We look for independent evidence and test tools in our own classes before adopting them widely.
Every activity has an offline alternative, so learners without devices are not excluded.
We review this policy every year.

blocks.x: This generalizes the AI conclusion of Unit 84: value where the evidence and the match are good, caution everywhere else.

body: Purpose: to show evidence-responsive judgement. Content: a balance scale; on one pan ‘real benefits in well-matched uses’, on the other ‘limited evidence, cost, equity’, with a teacher adjusting the pivot. Style: calm. Board version: a simple scale.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared policy draft.

blocks.x: A printed policy on the staff notice board.

body: Choose one app or platform your learners use. Find one independent study of it, or of tools like it, and one piece of evidence from your own class. Write three sentences: what it is good for, what it is not good for, and what you will do differently.

dek: Unit 93 of 100: the evidence base behind AI tutors, adaptive learning platforms, and educational technology more broadly — separating genuine findings from marketing claims.

aims.x: Every year brings new apps, platforms and AI tools that promise faster, easier English learning. Some deliver real benefits; many promise more than the evidence supports. This unit gives teachers and teacher educators the tools to tell the difference. It applies the critical research reading of Unit 81 and the balanced AI stance of Unit 84 to educational technology as a whole, and it shows how a teacher can gather their own evidence through a small, careful pilot.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: distinguish vendor claims from independent research evidence;
summarize what research suggests about adaptive platforms, AI conversation partners and gamified apps;
match a tool to the kind of learning it can realistically support;
evaluate a new tool with a structured checklist and a small classroom pilot;
explain how teacher beliefs and school culture shape technology adoption;
design a simple delayed test to check whether learning lasts;
write a balanced, evidence-responsive technology policy for a department or DIET.

why: Why this matters. Educational technology is heavily marketed, often outpacing the actual research evidence supporting specific tools' claimed effectiveness.

background.x: Enthusiasm for educational technology has a long history, and so does disappointment. Larry Cuban (2001) found that computers placed in American schools were often ‘oversold and underused’: bought with high hopes, then used in ways that changed little. Richard Clark (1983) argued, controversially, that media themselves do not cause learning; the method of instruction delivered through them does. Clark’s view is still debated, but his warning remains useful: when a study credits ‘the app’ with a gain, we should ask what learners actually did differently.

Research on computer-assisted language learning is large but uneven. Syntheses have found generally positive effects, with wide variation between tools, tasks and contexts, and have noted that many studies are short and small (Plonsky and Ziegler 2016). Indian evidence is instructive. A randomized study of the adaptive Mindspark programme in Delhi after-school centres found substantial gains in mathematics and Hindi over a few months (Muralidharan, Singh and Ganimian 2019), while an earlier study of computer-assisted mathematics in Vadodara found that much of the gain faded after the programme ended (Banerjee et al. 2007) [VERIFY extent of fade-out]. Neither study was about English, but both show that design, implementation and duration matter more than the label ‘technology’.

NEP 2020 encourages the use of technology in teaching, learning and assessment, while noting the digital divide and the need to evaluate technology carefully before scaling it (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). Indian teachers already work with platforms such as DIKSHA and with apps learners bring from home. In classes of 40–60 learners, with one shared phone per family, the question is rarely ‘Should we use technology?’ but ‘Which use, for which learners, and with what evidence?’ This unit answers that question with the same rigour we would apply to any other research claim.

items: Claim analysis. An evaluation of one vendor claim with an honest rewrite.
Pilot report. A short report on a local tool pilot with a baseline, a comparison and a decision.
Retention evidence. Delayed-test results for one unit and a reflection on what supported retention.
Policy. A department or DIET technology policy with evidence-based principles and offline alternatives.
Which technology have you adopted because it was available rather than because it was needed?
How do you distinguish learners’ enjoyment from their learning?
What evidence would persuade you to stop using a tool you like?
Which learners in your class are left out by the technology you use?
How do your beliefs about technology shape the way you use it?
What would a fair local pilot of a new tool look like in your school?

reading: Banerjee, A. V., S. Cole, E. Duflo, and L. Linden. 2007. ‘Remedying education: evidence from two randomized experiments in India’. Quarterly Journal of Economics 122/3: 1235–64.
Clark, R. E. 1983. ‘Reconsidering research on learning from media’. Review of Educational Research 53/4: 445–59.
Cuban, L. 2001. Oversold and Underused: Computers in the Classroom. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.
Deci, E. L., R. Koestner, and R. M. Ryan. 1999. ‘A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation’. Psychological Bulletin 125/6: 627–68.
Ertmer, P. A. and A. T. Ottenbreit-Leftwich. 2010. ‘Teacher technology change: how knowledge, confidence, beliefs, and culture intersect’. Journal of Research on Technology in Education 42/3: 255–84.
Ministry of Human Resource Development. 2020. National Education Policy 2020. New Delhi: Government of India.
Muralidharan, K., A. Singh, and A. J. Ganimian. 2019. ‘Disrupting education? Experimental evidence on technology-aided instruction in India’. American Economic Review 109/4: 1426–60.
Plonsky, L. and N. Ziegler. 2016. ‘The CALL–SLA interface: insights from a second-order synthesis’. Language Learning & Technology 20/2: 17–37. [VERIFY pages]
perm: Do not ask learners to enter personal information into AI tools, and follow each tool’s age restrictions.

All claims, logs, pilot summaries, results and belief statements are written for this book; the classes are fictional. Product names are trademarks of their owners. Screenshots of Anki, Quizlet, Kahoot!, Wayground, ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, DIKSHA or Google tools require permission or replacement with original illustrations. Follow each tool’s age limits and data-protection terms.

terms.def: Digital instruction in which software adjusts the content, difficulty or pace of tasks according to each learner’s responses; its claims should be checked against independent evidence before a school adopts it.
A test given some time after an intervention to check whether learning has lasted, not just appeared immediately afterwards; it is important when evaluating claims made for new methods or technology.

The digital and non-digital tools used to support teaching and learning, from projectors and apps to learning platforms such as DIKSHA. Its value depends on purpose and pedagogy rather than on the tool itself.
A reward that comes from outside the activity, such as points, badges or prizes. In gamified learning it can raise short-term participation but may weaken interest in the activity itself.

An external obstacle to using technology in teaching, such as lack of devices, connectivity or time. It contrasts with second-order barriers, which are teachers’ beliefs and confidence (Ertmer and Ottenbreit-Leftwich 2010).
Adding game elements such as points, levels, badges and leaderboards to learning activities to increase motivation. Its benefits depend on whether the language work itself remains central.

A small-scale trial run of a research study, carried out to test instruments such as questionnaires, and procedures such as timing, before the main study; problems found are fixed before full data collection.

An obstacle to technology use that lies in teachers’ beliefs about teaching and learning, confidence and school culture, rather than in devices, connectivity or time, which are first-order barriers (Ertmer and Ottenbreit-Leftwich 2010).
Reviewing items, especially vocabulary, at gradually increasing intervals, just as they are about to be forgotten. Many flashcard apps schedule reviews automatically using this principle.
A claim made by a company about the effectiveness of its product, such as an app or platform. Teachers should distinguish vendor claims from independent research evidence and test them locally.
